vignette: The rain starts when the knife presses into his ribs. It is a Tuesday in November, three years ago, outside his apartment building in the city. He carries his weekend bag, keys in hand, when a figure steps from the alleyway. The demand is short, the blade sharp and cold. When he drops his wallet, a second attacker lunges, twisting his arm until his shoulder pops. He remembers the smell of wet asphalt and old copper, the way his breath hitches into silent sobs, and the sudden, suffocating realization that he is not going to stop them. They run. He stands on the corner until the streetlights flicker on, his hands shaking so violently he cannot unzip his coat. In the months that follow, the neighborhood he has walked for decades becomes a map of threats. He stops at every corner, scanning the space between buildings, counting exits before entering a room. Sleep fractures into fragments. His wife wakes to find him sitting upright in bed, eyes wide, breath shallow, as if listening for footsteps that never come. He checks the deadbolt six times before leaving the house. He stops taking the subway. He stops smiling in his sleep. The world narrows to what could go wrong. At the salon, the rhythm of his hands used to be his language. For twenty-two years, he has shaped hair, read moods through posture, and built quiet trust in the space between chair and mirror. Now, the clippers feel like foreign objects in his grip. He flinches when the doorbell chimes. He keeps the client's cape draped lower than necessary, creating a thick barrier of nylon between his skin and theirs. When a customer reaches suddenly to adjust a strand near his ear, his pulse jumps to his throat. He tells himself he is just being careful, but his mind races with calculations: the weight of the shears, the distance to the door, the nearest exit. He works slower now. He cancels more appointments. He tells his wife it is a rough season, but the truth is heavier. The scissors feel heavy in his hand, and he catches himself staring at the empty chair next to his, wondering who will sit there next, wondering if they will need him to turn around, to lower his guard, to trust. He starts the session with a deliberate, measured pace, giving himself time to verify that the room is clear, that the street is quiet, that nothing will change in the next ten minutes. At home, he moves through the rooms like a guest. He watches the street from the window while his wife folds laundry. He remembers the mugger's voice, not as a memory but as a sound that arrives unbidden in the grocery store, in his car, in the quiet between radio stations. He tries to breathe through it, to anchor himself in the familiar weight of the wedding band on his finger, but the body does not listen to logic. His shoulders stay tight, his jaw clenches, and he finds himself scanning faces in the park, looking for the posture of threat in strangers. He loves his wife deeply, but he pulls away when she touches his back, not from rejection, but from the sheer effort of staying present. The world feels both too close and too far. He sits in the waiting room of his own life, waiting for the next sound, the next shadow, the next reminder that safety was something he lost long before the knife appeared.
